passage:
Week one of October. Mohit's badminton coach, Sudha ma'am, filmed his smash again. Same speed on the tracker as in August. He had practised every morning. He stared at the number and thought, maybe this is it. Maybe this is my limit.
Week four. Still the same number. Mohit started leaving practice early, dragging his racket along the court floor. "I'm not improving, ma'am. I'm just not built for this."
Sudha ma'am said nothing. She pulled up two videos side by side, August and today. "Look at your feet." In August he had been flat-footed, lunging late. Now he was on his toes, arriving early under the shuttle.
Week six. In a practice match, Mohit returned three smashes he would have missed in the summer, without even thinking. The smash number hadn't changed. But on the bus home he replayed the rally and realised he had been getting better all along, just not where he was looking.

qa.q: What did Sudha ma'am tell Mohit to look at in the videos?
qa.a: His feet.

qa.q: Why did Mohit think he had hit his limit in October?
qa.a: His smash speed showed the same number as in August despite daily practice, so he read no visible change as no progress at all.

qa.q: What did Sudha ma'am do that helped Mohit through the plateau?
qa.a: She put his August and current videos side by side to show hidden progress in his footwork, instead of arguing with him.

qa.q: What might Sudha ma'am have been thinking when Mohit said he wasn't built for this?
qa.a: She likely knew his footwork had improved and chose to show him rather than tell him, trusting the evidence to change his mind.

grounding: Shows a teenager on a badminton plateau who suspects he has reached his limit while his footwork has quietly improved.

passage:
Trisha, you're sulking because your Kathak footwork feels stuck? Sit. Let your Ojas Tauji tell you about a typewriter.
When I was fifteen, in Kanpur, Babuji sent me to Sharma-ji's typing institute so I could get a clerk's job one day. In the first month I went from nothing to twenty-five words a minute. I thought I'd be a champion by summer. Then I reached thirty, and there I stayed. Two whole months. Thirty, thirty, thirty.
I told Babuji I had no talent for it and wanted to stop. Sharma-ji, a strict old man, pulled out my test sheets from the first month and from the last week. Yes, my speed was the same. But my errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two. "Your hands learned something your stopwatch couldn't see," he said.
The next month I jumped to forty.
So, beta, your feet are learning something too. You just can't see it yet.

qa.q: What speed did Ojas get stuck at for two months?
qa.a: Thirty words a minute.

qa.q: Why did Ojas tell Babuji he had no talent for typing?
qa.a: His speed stayed at thirty for two months, so he felt discouraged and believed he had reached his limit.

qa.q: How did Sharma-ji reveal the hidden progress, and what could Trisha try?
qa.a: He compared early and recent test sheets, showing errors had fallen from fourteen a page to two; Trisha could compare old and new Kathak recordings to spot hidden gains in the footwork.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel hearing Tauji's typewriter story?
qa.a: Trisha may feel less alone and more hopeful that the stuck footwork is still improving under the surface.

grounding: Illustrates, through an uncle's memory of a typing plateau, how progress can continue beneath the surface when no visible change shows.

passage:
In the small town of Malerkotla, Nazia had been practising Urdu calligraphy every evening for two months. The first month, every week was better. Now, for four weeks, her letters looked exactly the same.
"Maybe this is as good as I get," she told her friend Trisha, putting the pen down.
Trisha picked up Nazia's very first practice sheet from the drawer, then put it next to today's. "Look."
Nazia looked. The old letters wobbled. The new ones were steady, the curves smoother.
"But I didn't see it happening."
"That's how it works," Trisha said. "You don't notice, but it's going on anyway."

qa.q: How long had Nazia been practising calligraphy?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she put the pen down?
qa.a: Nazia felt discouraged, worried she had reached her limit after four weeks of no visible change.

qa.q: What did Trisha do that helped?
qa.a: She placed Nazia's first sheet next to today's, showing the progress she hadn't noticed.

qa.q: What might Trisha be feeling as Nazia compares the sheets?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels pleased and encouraging, glad to show Nazia her hidden progress.

grounding: Shows a teen whose calligraphy seems stuck and who fears a limit, until an old sheet reveals improvement under the surface.

passage:
In Kyiv, Nadia had been swimming lengths every morning for three months. The first weeks, her times dropped fast. Now, for five weeks, they hadn't moved at all.
She climbed out of the pool, frustrated. "I've hit my ceiling," she told her coach, Ivan.
"Show me your breathing."
She swam a length. Ivan nodded. "In September, you gasped every two strokes. Now you breathe every four, smoothly. That's progress. It's just not on the stopwatch yet."
Nadia frowned. "It doesn't feel like progress."
"It rarely does, on a plateau. Keep going. The times will follow."

qa.q: How often did Nadia gasp in September?
qa.a: Every two strokes.

qa.q: What was Nadia feeling when she climbed out of the pool?
qa.a: Nadia felt frustrated and discouraged, believing she had hit her ceiling.

qa.q: What did Ivan do that helped Nadia see her progress?
qa.a: He pointed to her improved breathing, a hidden change not yet shown on the stopwatch.

qa.q: How does Ivan see Nadia's plateau?
qa.a: Ivan sees it as a normal stage where progress happens under the surface, and feels confident her times will improve.

grounding: Shows a teen swimmer on a plateau who fears a ceiling, while her coach points out hidden improvement.

passage: At the district sports hostel, the long-jump pit had become Jeevan's least favourite place. For six weeks the tape had shown the same mark, give or take a few centimetres. Same run-up, same takeoff board, same thud into the sand. Every evening he wrote the number in his notebook, and every evening it looked like a wall. Maybe this is it, he thought, raking the sand harder than he needed to. Maybe this is as far as my legs go. Mridul, who trained in the next lane, jogged over. "Your takeoff looks different from last month, you know. Less of a stutter." Jeevan shrugged. He couldn't see it. All he could see was the number that wouldn't move.

qa.q: How long had the tape shown the same mark?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's raking the sand so hard suggest about his mood?
qa.a: He feels frustrated and discouraged, suspecting he has hit his limit.

qa.q: What could help Jeevan see past the plateau?
qa.a: Asking the coach to film his takeoff and compare it with last month would show changes the tape number hides.

qa.q: What does Mridul notice that Jeevan cannot?
qa.a: Mridul sees a smoother takeoff with less stutter, progress happening under the surface while the number stays still.

grounding: Shows a teen athlete stuck at the same mark for weeks, reading no visible change as a limit while improvement happens underneath.
